title: Development of a constant load test to determine the liquid metal embrittlement susceptibility of advanced high-strength steels
abstract: Abstract Liquid metal embrittlement (LME) poses a challenge in resistance spot welding (RSW) of high-strength steels. The diffusion of zinc along the steel’s grain boundaries leads to a loss of ductility and premature material fractures. To test steel grades for LME susceptibility, RSW tests and hot tensile tests (HTT) have been developed. However, these methods sometimes fail to differentiate accurately. This study introduces a constant load test (CLT) and evaluates its feasibility as alternative test method for assessing LME susceptibility. The current work is conducted using a thermomechanical simulator, with specific settings developed for testing. Three steel grades are examined within a balanced preload range. The test speed being a dynamic parameter is measured at up to 180 mm/s during fracture. Temperature and elongation are correlated dependent on the preload, allowing better differentiation of steels compared to the standard HTT. Additionally, key values are derived to estimate LME susceptibility as relation of uncoated and Zn-coated samples.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: For the successful product launch of newly developed advanced high-strength steels with improved ductility (3 rd  Gen AHSS), processing technology—in this case, welding technology—poses a significant challenge. Even conventional resistance spot welding (RSW) faces a critical issue due to liquid metal embrittlement (LME) induced cracks [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. Studies show that LME occurs because of Zn penetrating grain boundaries (GB) by diffusion, a process intensified by stress and temperature [ 4 ,  5 ]. The formation of Zn-Fe phases within the GB leads to local stresses, which initiates crack formation [ 4 ]. Liquid Zn may fill surface cracks, but it primarily aids the GB diffusion process [ 5 ,  6 ]. Four prerequisites are necessary for LME to occur: prolonged contact between liquid Zn and the solid substrate, high-energy GB, applied tensile stress, and crack propagation that outpaces protective phase formation. During the melting and diffusion of Zn within the steel substrate, Zn-Fe phases are formed, which can either have a protective or a harmful nature. Protective phases are known to be the δ- and the Γ-phase of the Zn-Fe phase diagram, if they form a dense and continuous layer, they are preventing Zn diffusion [ 7 ]. However, Zn-rich ferrite (αFe(Zn)), which grows globular, likely makes the material more prone to LME by enabling rapid diffusion along its GBs [ 8 ,  9 ].

The susceptibility of a material, i.e., a steel grade, to LME depends on multiple factors. The microstructure of the base material, such as GB size and the presence of prior austenite grain boundaries, plays a significant role, as shown in multiple studies [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. In general, a high content of ignoble alloying elements can increase LME sensitivity [ 1 ]. Among the alloying elements, silicon and boron are particularly relevant in the context of LME. Numerous studies indicate that a high silicon content increases susceptibility, as it slows the Zn-Fe phase reaction and thereby delays the formation of protective intermetallic layers [ 13 ,  14 ]. This is why 3 rd  Gen AHSS grades with elevated silicon content are especially prone to LME. Boron, on the other hand, exhibits the opposite effect. Although the mechanism is not yet fully understood, this element appears to reduce LME susceptibility by segregating at the GBs and therefore hindering Zn-diffusion along the GBs [ 15 ,  16 ]. In terms of processing parameters, the Zn-coating method itself can also have a notable impact. For instance, hot-dip galvanized (GI) materials are generally more susceptible to LME than electrogalvanized (EG) materials [ 1 ,  17 ].

Testing and evaluate the occurrence of LME severe conditions need to be established. Therefore, a RSW test has been developed to provoke cracks by means of exaggerated heat input, classifying steels as LME sensitive or LME insensitive [ 18 ,  19 ]. Additionally, LME sensitivity is occasionally tested with Gas Metal Arc Brazing and Welding [ 20 ]. The welding process involves complex variables like temperature and deformation, best approximated through FE simulations [ 18 ].

The hot tensile test (HTT) has become a popular method for studying LME sensitivity, because it allows controlled temperature and stress conditions relevant to welding. Standardized by the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA), the HTT examines the reduction in ductility of zinc-coated materials compared to uncoated ones. The test cycle includes heating, holding, and tensile testing at elevated temperatures (600–900 °C). A thermomechanical simulator has been recommended for testing under defined conditions to provide robust results when the prescribed test is followed [ 21 ]. According to the VDA procedure, the heating rate should be 1000 K/s, the holding time should be 1 s, and the strain rate should be 3 mm/s [ 21 ,  22 ]. HTT serves as a pre-assessment for LME sensitivity, with specific key values extracted from the obtained curves presenting the force dependent on the stroke [ 21 ].

Both welding tests and the hot tensile test (HTT) have advantages and disadvantages. The HTT is easier to describe and provides more precise load data. Nevertheless, both tests are often needed to fully assess a material’s LME susceptibility [ 21 ]. Some materials exhibit LME sensitivity in welding, whereas the HTT cannot proof such, and vice versa. This discrepancy is highlighted in Steineder et al.’s study [ 19 ], which compared boron-modified steel with non-modified steel. The boron-alloyed material showed better LME resistance in a RSW test. However, a clear distinction within the HTT in favor of the boron-alloyed sample was only possible at an extremely high strain rate of 100 mm/s. The subsequent problem that arises from this is the limitation concerning the strain rate imposed by the thermomechanical simulator [ 19 ]. Furthermore, results of the HTT can vary based on heating rates, as it was shown in Kim et al.’s study [ 23 ] where they showed that lower heating rates lower the LME susceptibility. Also, holding times can have an influence according to Sage and Fink’s study [ 24 ]. The strain rate seems to be a decisive factor for the LME susceptibility as well. Kang et al. [ 25 ] concluded that slow strain rates decrease LME susceptibility. Similar outcomes were shown in the studies of Beal et al. [ 26 ], Pant et al. [ 27 ], and Bhattacharya et al. [ 28 ].

To improve comparability, a new test procedure is developed, in which such influences do not play a significant role. Instead, the testing procedure should more closely reflect actual conditions similar to the RSW test. The constant load test (CLT) promises exactly these characteristics. The CLT is designed to investigate material behavior under a continuous applied load while being gradually heated until failure. In this paper, three materials are compared, results are discussed, and details of the test procedure are presented.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The primary material investigated is a 3rd generation AHSS with high strength and enhanced formability, that consists of a trip-bainitic-ferritic (TBF) matrix and a certain amount of stabilized retained austenite at room temperature. It will be referred to as TBF1180. This material is generally recognized for its susceptibility to LME, particularly due to its high silicon content [ 7 ,  10 ]. To examine the beneficial influence of boron on the LME susceptibility of a high-silicon steel grade, a TBF1180 with added boron (TBF1180 + B) was included in the test program. Both steel grades were electrogalvanized (EG) with a Zn-coating thickness of around 8 µm.

To investigate the behavior of a material with low LME susceptibility, a rather common dual-phase steel will be used, referred to as DP800. The susceptibility of this material has been previously tested in various experiments [ 7 ,  10 ]. The product is hot-dip galvanized (GI) with a Zn-coating thickness of around 8 µm.

All samples are collected from large-scale coils having a thickness of 1.5 mm produced by the voestalpine Stahl GmbH. An excerpt from the chemical compositions of the steel grades is given in Table  1 . Mechanical properties after galvanization are listed in Table  2 .
 Table 1 Excerpt from the chemical composition and transition temperatures of the used steel grades C [wt.-%] Si [wt.-%] Mn [wt.-%] B [ppm] A c1  [°C] A c3  [°C] TBF1180 0.20 1.5  < 3.0 - 720 720 TBF1180 + B 0.20 1.5  < 3.0 10–50 850 850 DP800 0.15 0.2  < 2.5 - 690 810 Table 2 Specified mechanical properties of the used steel grades Yield strength [MPa] Ultimate tensile strength [MPa] Elongation at fracture A 80  [%] TBF1180  > 850  > 1180  > 13 TBF1180 + B  > 850  > 1180  > 13 DP800  > 440  > 780  > 14

The galvanization can either be electrogalvanized or hot dip galvanized, depending on the specific steel grade being tested. For comparison, samples without coatings are pickled after cutting to remove any zinc, and these are referred to as uncoated (UC) samples. The pickling was done using a mixture of two-thirds water, one-third hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37% concentration), and 2 g/l of hexamethylenetetramine as inhibitor.

sections.heading: Sample preparation
paragraphs: For the CLT tests, a specific sample shape is required, and the panels were cut using a laser cutting machine. The standard shape of these samples follows the specifications recommended by van der Aa and the VDA workgroup on LME for the HTT [ 10 ], as shown in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Schematic depiction of the sample geometry including dimensions in mm [ 10 ]

sections.heading: Constant load test
paragraphs: The CLT described in this work was performed using the Gleeble® 3800 thermomechanical simulator manufactured by Dynamic Systems Inc. Given that no standardized setup exists for the CLT to measure LME susceptibility, extensive preliminary testing was required. This allowed for the identification of optimal parameters that ensured consistent tensile load application during heating, which is critical for accurately assessing LME behavior. The hydraulic system, typically used for controlling force during tests such as the hot tensile test (HTT), was decoupled as due to its inertia it is too slow in adopting to the load. Instead, a pneumatic system known as the Air Ram was used to apply the constant tensile load. The Air Ram is able to react quickly enough to maintain the load during the rapid heating process, compensating for any expansion of the sample as its temperature increases. This modification was essential for capturing the accurate LME response of the materials under investigation.

Preloads chosen for the CLT ranges from 2 to 6 kN, corresponding to the yield strength of the tested materials given above. A uniform range of preloads is used for all steel grades to prove the comparability of different materials with the CLT. Testing within this preload range should provide a testing window to highlight LME susceptibility.

Once the Air Ram is calibrated to apply the desired constant load, the sample is heated at a rate of 300 K/s. The decision on the heating rate was based on preliminary trials. It is difficult to draw direct comparisons or base parameter selection strictly on existing studies as this specific test setup and evaluation method have not been previously reported in the literature. As such, the chosen heating rate represents a balanced and practical choice. Maintaining the desired preload during heating causes fluctuation of the force (noise), which remains in a range smaller than ± 0.2 kN. As the sample is heated, its yield strength decreases, eventually leading to failure. After the sample fractures, it is air quenched and the test ends. The force applied and the elongation (L-gauge) of the sample are continuously recorded during the test. The temperature is measured by a thermocouple of type K welded onto the middle of the sample as seen in Fig.  1 . The test procedure as well as the measurement curves are shown schematically in Fig.  2 . The parameters are kept consistent across all samples and tests. For each preload level, two samples are tested: one with a Zn-coating and one without. Fig. 2 Schematic depiction of the testing procedure for the CLT as force, temperature, and elongation of the sample over the test time

The data recordings give detailed insight in the evolution of force, temperature, and elongation as a function of the testing time. Because LME is understood as a loss of ductility, elongation at fracture would be the most obvious key measurements here. However, analyzing maximum values poses challenges. The exact fracture moment can be difficult to pinpoint, particularly when thermocouples display inaccurate readings at the point of fracture due to their placement on detached parts of the broken samples. Additionally, the measured force approaches the x-axis asymptotically, making fracture identification inaccurate. Furthermore, in this range, the elongation accelerates increasingly, which also decreases the resolution and quality of the measurements.

The testing speed is determined as the slope of the tangent to the elongation curve. It becomes evident that the slope of the tangent and thus the speed multiplies rapidly during fracture. Conversely, tensile test speed is significantly lower in the elastic range of sample elongation. This behavior underscores the dynamic nature of the deformation process. For this reason, the tensile test speed was measured and evaluated at 50% loss of preload. This approach is intended to provide a representative average value, offering a useful overview of the tensile test speed behavior. Furthermore, the values of temperature and elongation were evaluated at 50% loss of the initial preload. This can be compared to the standard procedure in the HTT where the “stroke at 50% loss of max. tensile force” is used for further evaluation. Consequently, “temperature at 50% loss of preload” and “elongation at 50% loss of preload” were evaluated and for the sake of simplicity will simply be referred to as “fracture temperature” and “fracture elongation.”

sections.heading: Testing speed and the advantage of CLT
paragraphs: One key motivation for the CLT, in contrast to the established HTT, was to develop a test procedure where preloaded samples will deform in a more natural manner, similar to the actual resistance spot welding. There, an electrode is pressed onto a material at ambient temperature inducing compressive stresses, and subsequently, only the induced current flow increases the temperature through Joule heating. Consequently, the electrodes penetrate further and form a thermal bridge to deeper, overheated areas, which are then rapidly quenched.

As introduced above, the HTT proved to be too slow to clearly distinguish between TBF1180 and TBF1180 + B. Figure  3  illustrates the tensile test speeds at 50% loss of preload for the three steel grades at various preloads. A noticeable drop in tensile test speed can be seen for the TBF1180 + B at 3 kN. This drop remains unexplained as due to the low sampling quantity scattering cannot be quantified at this point. Ignoring the scatter, the final evaluated test speed increases with higher preload, in fact, reaching up to 180 mm/s. Therefore, the prerequisite of a sufficiently fast enough testing speed proposed by Steineder et al. [ 19 ] is accomplished. Fig. 3 Tensile test speed dependent on the preload for indicated steel grades uncoated (UC) or coated (EG/GI)

A proper explanation of the increased tensile test speeds for uncoated samples within one material and especially for higher preloads need to be connected to the aspect of fracture temperature and fracture elongation and shall be elaborated in detail later on.

sections.heading: Influence of preload on fracture temperature and fracture elongation
paragraphs: Figure  4  depicts the fracture temperature dependent on the preload for the 3 tested steel grades in coated and uncoated state. Higher preloads consistently result in lower fracture temperatures for all tested steels and coating states and uncoated samples never show lower fracture temperatures than coated ones. At higher preloads, the fracture temperatures of coated and uncoated samples converge. Fig. 4 Fracture temperature of the indicated steel grades uncoated (UC) or coated (EG/GI)

The fracture elongations over the preload of the tested materials are shown in Fig.  5 . It is obvious, that uncoated samples exhibit higher values, than their coated counterparts, whereupon the gap decreases with rising preloads. The preload itself has a diverse effect on the 3 different steel grades and coating states. Uncoated samples exhibit a considerable loss in fracture elongation with rising preload, except the DP800 which shows a sudden drop at 2 kN. Coated samples demonstrate tremendously smaller fracture elongations for TBF1180 and still declines gently with rising preloads. TBF1180 + B follows this trend at low preloads but exhibits a noticeable rise in fracture elongation at 5 kN preload. DP800 behaves differently: It shows a drop at 2 kN similar to its uncoated counterpart and the values for coated and uncoated samples almost align at preloads of 4 kN and above. Fig. 5 Fracture elongation for indicated steel grades uncoated (UC) or coated (EG/GI)

The difference of the fracture elongation between coated and uncoated samples of all three tested materials converge at higher preloads. While TBF1180 still shows a significant difference between coated and uncoated under high preloads, this difference is already reduced in its boron-added counterpart. For DP800, no difference between coated and uncoated samples are observed for preloads above 4 kN. Such a decreasing difference in fracture temperature and fracture elongation between coated and uncoated samples indicates a reduced deterioration due to LME. Or vice versa and more understandable, a higher difference between coated and uncoated samples indicates an increased LME susceptibility.

Additionally, it stands out that coated samples generally fail at lower temperatures than the uncoated counterparts. This can be explained by the formation of LME-induced cracks, which start to propagate and cause earlier fracture of the samples. Of course, this is evident in the smaller fracture elongation values too. In absence of such a deteriorating effect such as LME, uncoated samples on the other hand will be heated up farther until excessive elongation starts due to material softening.

Higher preloads cause an increase in the tensile test speed (see Fig.  3 ), and therefore, even for uncoated samples a stable necking of the material cannot take place anymore which leads to rupture at lower elongations. For coated samples, it is worth to mention that LME is a stress induced phenomenon, so higher preloads lead also to higher stresses along the interface between the steel and the Zn-coating causing formation of more LME-induced cracks and their further and faster propagation as well.

sections.heading: Linking of temperature and elongation
paragraphs: To establish an understanding of the very moment a sample ruptures in the CLT, it becomes necessary to combine the effects of fracture temperature and fracture elongation, both dependent on the preload as described above. Figure  6  presents fracture elongation plotted against fracture temperature. This visualization enables a more comprehensive interpretation of the phenomenon taking place. First it needs to be addressed, that it is not possible to calculate a difference in fracture elongation at a certain temperature directly, because the later changes also, depending on the underlying preload. Linear interpolation could be a method of choice. Instead, one may rather perform a qualitative interpretation and focus on the evolving gap between the fracture elongation for uncoated and coated samples. The further these lines drift apart from each other, the more severe the LME-impairment becomes in this temperature region. Fig. 6 Fracture elongation vs. fracture temperature of indicated steel grades at indicated preload levels for uncoated and coated samples

Another interesting feature of this visualization is that the lateral shift of the fracture temperatures depending on the underlying preload becomes visible too. Therefore, some measurements of fracture elongation could be compared at similar fracture temperatures, which in turn are based on samples of different preloads.

For TBF1180, a significant gap in the fracture elongation between coated and uncoated samples is evident, with coated samples showing only little elongation throughout all preloads and fracture temperatures. In fact, this demonstrates the material’s LME sensitivity for all preloads and fracture temperatures. The low elongation values of coated specimens, regardless of the temperature, underline the severe embrittling effect zinc has on this steel under all tested conditions.

For the boron-modified TBF1180 + B, the trends of the uncoated samples are similar to those of the unmodified pendant, confirming the test’s validity. While the values for the coated samples at smaller preloads (equal to higher fracture temperatures) remain nearly identical, a more noticeable difference emerges at higher preload levels (equal to lower fracture temperatures). At a preload of 5 kN and above (corresponding to fracture temperatures below 700 °C), a significant increase in fracture elongation is observed for the coated sample. Therefore, the LME sensitivity of TBF1180 + B is lower than of TBF1180. This statement, as previously mentioned, is also supported by findings in the literature. For example, the papers by Shajan et al. [ 15 ], Steineder et al. [ 19 ] and Akbari et al. [ 16 ] all show that the addition of Boron reduces the crack length in RSW by lowering the GB energy, which in turns mitigates LME [ 10 ,  16 ]. This reduced crack length due to less LME makes itself noticed as reduced difference to the uncoated sample in the case of the CLT. Therefore, the CLT, in its testing approach, is capable of confirming what the HTT can only demonstrate with great difficulty, but certainly not within the testing dynamics recommended by the VDA [ 21 ]. At the same time, the testing procedure remains simpler than the RSW test.

Though DP800 is different in microstructure and strength to the TBF1180/+ B, its comparison provides valuable insights. At high preloads of 4kN and above (equal to fracture temperatures below 700 °C), fracture elongation differences between coated and uncoated samples are negligible, suggesting no LME damage. This reflects the findings of van der Aa et al. [ 12 ] and Sierlinger et al. [ 18 ] which used the DP800 in RSW tests and HTT. Interestingly, the fracture elongation for DP800 begins to diverge above 700 °C. Therefore, it can be stated that such a material begins to become LME-susceptible when being austenitized. The magnitude of degradation can be estimated with the distance of the fracture elongation between coated and uncoated samples. Apparently, this difference increases with rising fracture temperature. The DP800 generally shows no LME sensitivity in HTT or RSW tests [ 12 ,  18 ]; however, internal investigations by means of gas metal arc brazing exhibited signs of LME and therefore support this indication merely the specific vulnerable temperature range is different.

Thus, the key findings are that CLT with high preloads can distinct steel types with higher and lower LME sensitivities by the gap between coated and uncoated values. The HTT as standard method used for testing materials for its LME susceptibility could not prove this effectively as shown in Steineder et al.’s [ 19 ] study. As said before, only high strain rates can accomplish the differentiation, but such rates are not always guaranteed to be reached by the thermomechanical simulator in case of a HTT. However, as shown above, the CLT proves to be fast enough, which form the broader context of this discussion. As shown in Fig.  3 , increasing preload results in a clear rise in testing speed, which is important since LME is stress- and strain-rate sensitive. This confirms that the applied testing conditions are dynamically severe enough to trigger LME where a material is susceptible.

Furthermore, the CLT method proves capable not only of distinguishing the relative LME resistance between the materials but also of localizing the critical temperature range where LME effects begin to dominate. On the one hand, these results confirm accompanying observations and on the other hand refine this awareness by localizing it to a temperature range, in this case to be below the transition temperature A c1 . It could be assumed, that below the austenitization temperature A c1 , the beneficial effect of free boron is by hindering Zn-diffusion along grain boundaries. In case of beginning austenitization, new grain boundaries evolve, which may be natively prone to LME, especially in the presence of such high temperatures.

Figure  6  essentially merges both Figs.  4  and  5 . It confirms the trend that higher preloads result in lower fracture temperatures across all steels. Importantly, coated samples consistently fracture at lower temperatures than their uncoated counterparts, strongly indicating that LME-induced cracks cause premature failure. The difference in elongation between coated and uncoated samples across temperatures and preloads emerges as a clear and practical metric for LME sensitivity. The CLT methodology, when combined with analysis of tensile speed, fracture temperature, and elongation, provides a comprehensive and localized understanding of LME susceptibility in different steels, fulfilling its intended role as a rapid and insightful test method for material screening.

sections.heading: Key value
paragraphs: Figure  7  illustrates the relative difference (Δ) in fracture elongation for all tested steel grades, as a function of the preload. The diagram depicting the difference in fracture elongation between coated and uncoated samples vs preload shows different behavior of the tested steels. The TBF1180 and TBF1180 + B demonstrate a comparable difference in fracture elongation for preloads below 5 kN, which corresponds to fracture temperatures above 700–750 °C. At preloads of 5kN and above the key value for these two steel grades diverges, indicating a different LME sensitivity. Even as a material not known to be LME-sensitive, the DP800 shows a certain degradation of the difference in fracture elongation below 4 kN, representing fracture temperatures above 750 °C. At preloads of 4 kN and above, and therefore at lower fracture temperatures, no degradation can be determined. This indicates that this material starts to be prone to LME above the A c1 -temperature. These findings highlight the importance of an austenite fraction for LME once more. The fact that the TBF1180, the boron-alloyed pendant, and a rather inconspicuous DP800 are clearly differentiable proves the significance of the CLT. Fig. 7 Key value of the CLT test of indicated steel grades dependent on the preload. Difference (Δ) between uncoated and coated samples in fracture elongation

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: The CLT, as conducted in this work, offers several advantages over the HTT. The following points summarize the important conclusions: CLT enables faster testing compared to the HTT: It was demonstrated that the tensile test speed in the CLT is significantly higher. Simpler test setup: CLT offers easier parameter control and requires fewer specimens compared to the HTT. Improved material differentiation: CLT can distinguish between similar steel grades (e.g., TBF1180 vs. TBF1180 + B), particularly at higher preload levels (5–6 kN). Early LME detection: Steels like DP800 showed signs of LME at lower preload levels (2–3 kN) in CLT, despite showing no such susceptibility in previous HTT-based studies from van der Aa et al. [ 21 ] Enhanced sensitivity to LME behavior: The CLT provides additional insight into LME trends that may go undetected with standard HTT speeds (e.g., 3 mm/s in the work of Steineder et al. [ 19 ]).

Despite these promising results, this methodology still has limitations. The reliability of individual data points, which was not the focus of this work, should be addressed in future studies to investigate the reproducibility and robustness of the methodology across a broader range of materials. The applicability of a CLT in replicating real RSW conditions, particularly with respect to the nature of the forces involved, remains a subject of critical discussion. However, similar limitations apply to the HTT, which also does not accurately reproduce RSW conditions such as holding time or deformation dynamics [ 29 ]. The CLT’s reliability and reproducibility across a broader spectrum of steel grades must be fully validated in a next step. At this stage, it should be considered a supplemental tool rather than a replacement for the HTT.

Further development should also aim to define standardized testing parameters and to assess the sensitivity of the CLT to variations in specimen geometry, surface conditions, and environmental factors. As the CLT was applied for LME investigations for the first time, there are no established standards for evaluating and interpreting the results. While a key-value such as fracture elongation at 50% loss of preload has proven useful, other key values (e.g . , at 95% force drop or in the range of 10 to 30%) could also be considered. Given the multidimensional nature of the CLT, correlating temperature and elongation seems to be necessary in any case to further understand the LME behavior of the samples. Additionally, efforts should be made to integrate the CLT more deeply into industrial quality assurance protocols, particularly where rapid and reliable assessments are required.

In summary, the CLT presents a fast, simple, and effective alternative for detecting LME in steels. Its ability to align with trends reported in the literature supports its potential validity. However, further experimental investigations are necessary to comprehensively establish its reliability and broader applicability. Even with its constraints, the CLT was able to clearly differentiate LME susceptibility between various steel grades, demonstrating its value and fulfilling the intended goal of the study. With continued development, the CLT could become a valuable addition to the current suite of LME testing methodologies.
